reason: The verb has one broad sense (put to the test) that English splits into 'test' and 'tempt', and the run splits it unevenly. Jesus' wilderness ordeal and Hebrews 2:18 and 4:15 are rendered 'tested', against tradition, while 1 Thessalonians 3:5 keeps 'tempted' even though its own note says the pressure is persecution. The title ὁ πειράζων is 'the tester' in Matthew 4:3 but 'the tempter' in 1 Thessalonians 3:5. Because chapters are translated separately, the test/tempt line and the title need fixing in one place.
sense: to put a person or God to the test, whether to prove character, to trap, or by pressure that could make someone fail; this entry also fixes where 'tempt' is used instead

alternates.when: The context makes inward enticement to sin the point rather than trial or proving: James 1:13-14 (desire, evil, luring), 1 Corinthians 7:5 (lack of self-control), Galatians 6:1. Also allowed for the finite verb in 1 Thessalonians 3:5 to keep the wordplay with 'the tempter'.
The substantive participle ὁ πειράζων is used as a title for the devil (Matthew 4:3; 1 Thessalonians 3:5). Use 'the tempter' in both places, not 'the tester'.
Phrasal variant of the default, where people presume on or provoke God, Christ or the Spirit (Acts 5:9; 15:10; 1 Corinthians 10:9; Hebrews 3:9), or wherever plain 'test' reads awkwardly.
2 Corinthians 13:5 only, where the verb is paired with δοκιμάζω and English needs two different verbs for self-scrutiny.
A separate sense: with an infinitive, meaning to attempt to do something (Acts 9:26; 16:7; 24:6).

rationale: The Greek verb means to put to the test. In the Greek Old Testament it is the ordinary word for God testing Israel and Israel testing God, and Jesus' forty days and the argument of Hebrews both draw on that background. Modern English 'tempt' has narrowed to 'entice to sin', which hides this link and sits badly with suffering and persecution contexts, so 'test' is the default. 'Tempt' is kept where enticement to sin is plainly the point, and 'the tempter' is kept as the title because 'the tester' is not natural English for the devil.
standard_view: Most translations use 'tempt' for the devil's approach to Jesus, for Hebrews 2:18 and 4:15, 1 Corinthians 10:13 and James 1:13-14, and 'test' for the Pharisees' questions, the testing of God, Abraham, and Revelation. Some recent versions and many commentators prefer 'test' in the wilderness narratives and in Hebrews. Standard lexicons recognise both 'test' and 'tempt' as contextual senses of the one verb, and it is disputed which fits the wilderness narrative and Hebrews 4:15 ('yet without sin'). 'The tempter' is the near-universal rendering of the title.
